Body mass at hatching for the Red-faced mousebird (Urocolius indicus) is remarkably low, with newly emerged chicks weighing approximately 2.7 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.7 grams]. This minimal initial mass corresponds to an incubation period that lasts 13 days [ab = 13 days] when eggs are maintained at a temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C], a relatively short developmental window compared with other cocial species of similar body size. The altricial nestlings depend entirely on bi-parental provisioning during the early post-hatching phase, and their rapid growth trajectory is fueled by frequent crop-milk and fruit deliveries from both adults. Field observations indicate that the majority of egg-laying occurs during the austral spring, when fruit availability peaks in the savanna and woodland habitats favored by this species. The precise timing of hatching appears to be synchronized with the onset of the rainy season, ensuring a dependable food supply for the developing chicks. The low hatchling mass may reflect an adaptive trade-off between clutch size and egg size, allowing females to allocate resources to a larger number of eggs per breeding attempt.

Under the stable thermal conditions typically experienced by active adults of this species, which center around 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones has been characterized. Fledging occurs at approximately 17 days after hatching [tx = approximately 17 days after hatching], a period that aligns with the 14 to 20 day range reported in the broader literature for mousebirds at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. By this age, the developing chicks have acquired sufficient flight feather maturation to achieve sustained flight and depart the nest. Gonadal maturation, however, follows a considerably longer timeline: puberty is reached at 51 days after hatching [tp = 51 days after hatching], marking the onset of reproductive activation at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This delay between fledging and sexual maturity likely reflects the extended period required for juvenile birds to perfect foraging skills and accumulate the lipid stores necessary to support a costly breeding effort. Post-fledging dispersal typically begins shortly after nest departure, with juveniles forming small, nomadic flocks that roam widely in search of fruiting trees.

Female Red-faced mousebirds attain a maximum adult body mass of 53.5 grams [Wwi = 53.5 grams], a value that places them among the larger members of the Coliidae family. This ultimate wet weight is achieved during the early breeding season, when females are at their heaviest due to ovarian follicle development and the storage of calcium reserves for eggshell formation. In contrast, males tend to be slightly lighter on average, though the degree of sexual size dimorphism is modest in this species. The substantial adult mass relative to the 2.7 gram hatchling mass underscores a roughly twenty-fold increase in body size over the course of development, a growth pattern typical of altricial birds that invest heavily in rapid post-natal growth. The energetic demands of reaching this adult mass are met through a diet dominated by fleshy fruits, supplemented by occasional leaf buds and flowers. Seasonal fluctuations in adult body mass have been documented, with individuals losing condition during the dry season when fruit resources become scarce.

The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild reaches 11 years [am = 11 years], a notable longevity for a bird of its body mass at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of active periods at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], basal metabolic rate was measured at 129 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 129 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the relatively low metabolic intensity characteristic of frugivorous birds. This comparatively modest metabolic expenditure may contribute to the species' extended lifespan by reducing oxidative damage over time. Senescence in older individuals manifests as a gradual decline in feather quality and reduced locomotor performance, though reproductive output remains relatively stable until the final year of life. The combination of a slow life history pace and a frugivorous diet aligns with predictions from comparative analyses, which have shown that fruit-eating birds tend to exhibit longer lifespans than insectivorous or granivorous species of equivalent size, likely due to reduced foraging effort and lower predation risk.

Reproductive output in the Red-faced mousebird is characterized by moderate fecundity and a single annual breeding cycle. Females lay between 1 and 7 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 7 eggs per clutch], though clutches of 3 to 4 eggs are most frequently observed in the field. A single clutch is produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch is produced each year], with the timing concentrated in the spring months. First reproduction is typically deferred until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a value recorded under the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] that characterizes the active period for this species. This delay between reaching sexual maturity at 51 days and actual first breeding at one year suggests that social or ecological constraints, such as territory acquisition or the formation of stable pair bonds, play a significant role in determining the onset of reproduction. Cooperative breeding has been observed in some populations, with older offspring occasionally assisting with nestling provisioning, though this behavior appears facultative rather than obligate.
